notes.body: Gratitude here isn't a feeling or a polite thank-you — it's a debt you repay by acting. Like a doctor who prescribes a cure: praising the doctor's brilliance heals nothing; you're only truly grateful when you take the medicine, on schedule, including the bitter doses. Thanking the teacher means obeying, practising, and passing the knowledge on.
notes.anchor: how a person thanks a teacher for three gifts at once

notes.body: A real gift isn't an object you put on a shelf and admire — it's a road. The call points to knowledge, knowledge points to practice, and practice stretches toward a limit you never exhaust. You can't thank a road with a word; you thank a road by walking it.
notes.anchor: a true gift is dynamic — it is a trajectory

notes.body: The Persian chases mirage after mirage across the desert, and meets his teacher only at the point where the last mirage dissolves into nothing. The lesson: as long as he believed the mirage was water he was still trusting his own illusions. Real clarity arrives only when the false hopes are completely exhausted — the ego has to be emptied before it can be filled.
notes.anchor: the mirage resolves into the nothing it always was

notes.body: 'The most excellent of deeds is giving life to the dead' — and the dead here are the ignorant, spiritually inert like a corpse. Once revived, the seeker asks: did this whole unbroken chain of transmission tear through the veil just so it could end with me? No — receiving the trust obliges you to pass it on. That is why he cannot rest; he must go and teach.
notes.anchor: giving life to the dead means teaching the ignorant
